article_text:
News

This Ron DeSantis Statue Can’t Take the Heat

The climate group 350 Action’s gallium statue began melting soon after being installed outdoors in Tallahassee on October 13.

A life-sized statue of Florida Governor Ron DeSantis began melting soon after the climate advocacy group 350 Action installed it in front of a crowd of DeSantis supporters in Tallahassee on Tuesday, October 13.

The transformation of the gallium statue, aptly titled "DENIAL," into a skeletal base highlighted the elected official's longstanding rejection of climate change as Floridians prepare to vote for who will be DeSantis's successor on November 3.

The statue's placard reads, "I am not a global warming person," quoting DeSantis's proclamation during his gubernatorial campaign in 2018, and includes a reference to his 2024 signing of House Bill 1645, an energy law that axed the phrase “climate change” from Florida statutes and ended requirements for state agencies to prioritize climate-friendly facilities , among other rollbacks.

"Just as state legislation used bureaucratic language to erase 'climate change' from public law, we used civic branding to the public to witness climate reality firsthand," a 350 Action spokesperson and organizer told Hyperallergic. "The reaction speaks for itself: you can't deny the physical laws of nature, and you can't argue with the public record."

article_text:
The search for the next James Bond may finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next British agent 007 this weekend.

According to the Hollywood Reporter and Variety , citing several sources, a group of actors reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.

The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die. Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.

Dune film-maker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (£6.9bn) deal in 2022. The Peaky Blinders writer Steven Knight will pen the script.

The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the next James Bond is under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”

In April of this year, Amazon film executives urged fans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision. “I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”

Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the beloved franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.

“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” he told Empire of Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December. “I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”

It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.

Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release.

article_text:
A feature by ArtThrob Editors on the 18th of July 2026. This should take you 3 minutes to read.

Every so often, curiosity gets the better of us, and we want to peer into the lives of others. So we reached out to artists, curators and practitioners at large to find out what books are keeping them busy this season. Here is what they had to say.

Olga Speakes , director at The AVA Gallery in Cape Town, recommended Arundhati Roy’s ‘Mother Mary Comes to Me ’ , an honest and insightful read into Roy’s life. Speakes is also inspired by a planned trip to Uzbekistan, the heart of the Silk Route trade, which will see her explore textile and fibre-based art. To enrich these experiences, she’s taking along ‘The Golden Thread: How Fabric Changed History’ by Kassia St. Clair. Her last recommendation is Vladimir Nabokov’s ‘Letters to Vera’ , edited by Olga Slonim and Brian Boyd. The book tells the story of a lifelong romance, the detritus of daily life and the experience of exile through personal correspondence by one of Russia’s most recognised literary giants.

Senior Director at Goodman Gallery, Jo Stella-Sawicka , enjoyed reading ‘ Carrie Mae Weems: The Heart of the Matter’ , edited by Sarah Meister, to accompany Carrie Mae Weems’ touring Aperture show. Including texts by friends, family, and colleagues from Dawoud Bey, Professor Deborah Willis, Elvira Dyangani Ose and Jeffrey Hoone, the book provides an intimate and insightful view of the artist’s four-decade-long career.

Another art book recommendation came from George Mahashe (associate professor at the Michaelis School of Fine Art, University of Cape Town) in the form of a scienticity reader of artistic, philosophical, theoretical moves on the epistemic instruments, ‘ Matter Mattering Matters’ . Edited by Kabelo Malatsie & Lantian Xie, the book brings together contributions by Karen Barad, Simnikiwe Buhlungu, Nolan Oswald Dennis, Rohini Devasher & Sabih Ahmed, Merve Ertufan, Ivana Franke, Jackie Karuti, George Mahashe, Sidony O’Neal, Raqs Media Collective, Oscar Santillan, Bogosi Sekhukhuni, and Aarti Sunder. Mahashe also recommended ‘Camera Geologica: An Elemental History of Photography’ by Siobhan Angus and Vusamazulu Credo Mutwa’s ‘Zulu Shaman: Dreams, Prophecies, and Mysteries’ as being top of his list.

Curator, researcher and editor Nisha Merit’s list was wide-ranging, including a historical novel ‘ The Art of Joy’ written by Goliarda Sapienza; ‘Freshwater’, the autobiographical fiction novel by Akwaeke Emezi; Olga Tokarczuk’s novel about travel, human anatomy, life, death, motion, migration, ‘ Flights’; ‘Land of Milk and Honey’ by C Pam Zhang as well as a book that was recommended to her that she just started reading; ‘Mating’ by Norman Rush.

Last but not least, we asked interdisciplinary artist Lerato Shadi what is on her list. She shared a picture with a table full of interesting titles, including ‘Xala’ – a satirical novel by Senegalese writer and filmmaker Ousmane Sembène, Zoe Wicomb’s ‘David’s Story’ , Bessie Head’s semi-autobiographical classic ‘A Question of Power’, Shannon Chakraborty’s ‘ The Adventures of Amina al-Sirafi’ , ‘Decolonising Methodologies’ by Linda Tuhiwai Smith, David Diop’s International Booker Prize winning ‘At Night All Blood is Black’ and ‘Unwinding Threads: Writing by Women in Africa’ edited by Charlotte H. Brunner.

article_text:
Sir Patrick Stewart, whose distinctive voice helped him embody everything from USS Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard to the X-Men’s Professor X to Ebenezer Scrooge to an emoji, has died .

His decades-long career spans the stage, the big screen, TV and commercials. He worked across genres from sci-fi to Shakespeare, to historical dramas to superhero films to comedy and animation.

RELATED: 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries

Scroll through the gallery below to see highlights from his wide and varied filmography.

article_text:
In “Father Country, I Do Love You”, on view at the Guggenheim in New York, Taryn Simon follows the life of an unnamed federal agent through 42 cases he worked on during his career. Together they become a thread for reflecting on American society and on the United States’ tentacular presence in other countries’ internal affairs.

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Taryn Simon.

Simon dedicates this body of work to her father, who worked abroad for the US government before switching to manufacturing pool tables and arcade games. She never heard his full story, and since his Alzheimer’s diagnosis she knows she never will. Because the agent is never named, he becomes one of countless people who carry out American policy, as Simon puts it, “without access to the entire picture.”

The exhibition raises questions about even the most solid values the country stands on. Democracy is one of them: a chapter traces it back to its origins in ancient Greece, in a reflection that echoes contemporary cases. “There was no prison, but if you were convicted you were kicked off a hill, which is very steep. If you survived, it meant you deserved a second chance.”

Photography is one of several media used to build a complex system of meaning. Text provides the context and, through the agent’s own words, sometimes exposes the failures of a system he never truly questions at its core. The photographs rely on their power to evoke, and they deliberately give up on explanations. Simon’s visual language is devoid of pathos even when she addresses a terrorist attack, a murder case or child pornography, and the power of the work comes from this restraint.

A game that visitors can play, recalling those Simon’s father once built, runs through the whole exhibition. In her words, ‘A single act of participation and touch unfolds in ways that can’t be calculated.’

The exhibition “Father Country, I Do Love You” is on view at the Guggenheim Museum in New York City until March 14, 2027.

title_original: At 96, Surrealist Painter Cossette Zeno Is Finally Having Her Moment
editorial_title_zh: 在96岁高龄，超现实主义画家科塞特·泽诺终于迎来了她的高光时刻
editorial_excerpt_zh: 当大多数人都在睡觉时，这位波多黎各艺术家仍在深夜挥动画笔。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这幅有点怪，”科塞特·泽诺（Cossette Zeno）指着她1952年的画作《我们去更高的地方》（Let’s Go Higher）说道。这幅画作于她求学期间——当时她还在圣胡安的波多黎各大学（University of Puerto Rico）读书——堪称一件真正的奇作。画面在一片薄雾笼罩的空旷风景中，排列着一组立方体。一群微小的人物攀爬着这些棱角分明的模块，其中大部分既没有窗户，也没有明显的实用功能。", "links": [{"text": "Cossette Zeno", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/cossette-zeno/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们在理查德·萨尔图恩（Richard Saltoun）的纽约画廊里见面，她目前在此举办一场聚焦其1950年代作品的小型回顾展。在那里，她引导我注意《我们去更高的地方》中唯一描绘有门洞的立方体。这座绿色建筑酷似一个散发着光芒的储物集装箱。一个孤立的身影站在立方体顶部，自豪地向周遭一切挥手示意。“他说的是：‘永远向上，绝不向下，’”泽诺微笑着说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这十分贴切地形容了泽诺的艺术生涯，它跨越了近一个世纪，直到最近几年才获得全球认可。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "96岁的泽诺曾在两场重大的超现实主义大展中大放异彩——一场是展现该运动全球化面貌的展览，于2021年至2022年在纽约大都会艺术博物馆（Metropolitan Museum of Art）和泰特现代美术馆（Tate Modern）展出；另一场则探索其加勒比分支，于2024年在德克萨斯州的沃斯堡现代艺术博物馆（Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth）展出。她的最新个展即理查德·萨尔图恩画廊的展览，将持续展出至周五。", "links": [{"text": "Surrealism", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/surrealism/"}, {"text": "a globalized version of the movement", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/artists/under-recognized-surrealists-met-museum-1234607237/"}, {"text": "its Caribbean strain", "url": "https://www.themodern.org/exhibition/surrealism-and-us-caribbean-and-african-diasporic-artists-1940"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在50年代，泽诺与超现实主义共同创始人安德烈·布勒东（André Breton）建立了联系，并曾与该运动的欧洲信徒们一同参展。然而，她从未获得经典地位，这或许是因为她的性别，亦或是由于许多西方艺术史学者有限的地理视野。此外，正如学者惠特尼·查德威克（Whitney Chadwick）所指出，许多女性超现实主义者并不认为自己是该运动的成员，部分原因在于她们对男性同僚产生了疏离感。这种边缘化感将梅特·奥本海姆（Meret Oppenheim）、利奥诺拉·卡林顿（Leonora Carrington）和雷梅迪奥斯·瓦罗（Remedios Varo）等画家排挤在外，而如今，她们都被视为超现实主义艺术史中不可或缺的人物。", "links": [{"text": "essential to Surrealist art history", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/artists/surrealism-art-masterpieces-1234713463/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，当我问及她如何定义自己的身份时，她告诉我：“我称自己为超现实主义者，因为我拥有他们那种自由的精神。我没有藩篱。我一直在进化，宝贝！”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Zeno_Ni-hablar-del-peluquin-No-Use-to-Talk-about-the-Little-Wig-…-1952.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一幅描绘了一团肉体纠缠在一起、顶部长着一簇头发的画作。", "caption": "科塞特·泽诺，《Ni hablar del peluquín (No Use to Talk about the Little Wig …) 》，1952年。图片由理查德·萨尔图恩画廊提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的超现实主义精神在《Ni hablar del peluquín (No Use to Talk about the Little Wig)》中得到了充分体现，这幅1952年的画作曾入选上述两场机构回顾展。画面展现了一团怪异纠缠的肉体，伴有几缕头发，这些头发既可能属于作品标题中的假发，也可能属于身体更为大胆私密的部位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“那代表了一个男人，”泽诺说。她注意到这幅画赤裸的色情意味，接着说道：“他在想很多事情——你可以自己决定他在想什么。他戴着假发，所以他已经不是年轻人了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萨尔瓦多·达利（Salvador Dalí）、马克斯·恩斯特（Max Ernst）和勒内·马格里特（René Magritte）等男性超现实主义者以将女性裸体描绘为欲望和阴谋的聚焦点而闻名。相比之下，泽诺估计自己只画过一次裸体女性。为什么？她开玩笑说：“我喜欢男人。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泽诺一边喝着啤酒，一边告诉我，这类作品都是在深夜创作的。时至今日，她仍然会在晚上11点开始创作，直到早晨7点才上床睡觉。“所有会打扰我的人都在睡觉，”她说。“我不用做饭，也不用打扫房子。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "许多超现实主义者将他们的作品比作梦境，这使得泽诺在他人处于快速眼动（REM）睡眠阶段时进行创作显得尤为引人注目。（这让人想起古巴超现实主义画家威尔弗雷多·拉姆[Wifredo Lam]曾经说过的一句话：“当我入睡时，我做梦。”）谈到自己深夜的艺术创作，泽诺告诉我：“我对自己正在做的事情完全清醒。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CZE094.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一幅以绿色背景衬托藤蔓状形态的画作。", "caption": "科塞特·泽诺，《Tropical Haze 》，1954年。摄影：查尔斯·鲁塞尔（Charles Roussel）", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泽诺于1930年出生于多米尼加共和国，当时正值拉斐尔·莱昂尼达斯·特鲁希略（Rafael Leónidas Trujillo）在动荡时期夺取政权后不久。在她牙牙学语时，泽诺和家人流亡并前往波多黎各。“我对圣多明各一点也不了解，”泽诺说，“这就是为什么我自称波多黎各人。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在老圣胡安，泽诺爱上了周围的山脉和大海。“无论你站在波多黎各的哪个地方，你都能看到海洋，”她说。“我外祖母过去常在早晨6点带我去海边，好让我能看到气泡里的小鱼。我以前经常浮潜。”随后，她补充道：“我与大自然非常亲近。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的一些早期作品便反映了这一点。两幅油画蜡笔画描绘了旋转的白色形态的组合；它们可能代表了在洋流中翻滚的贝壳。（泽诺是用从她父亲生意处得来的纸张创作的。）《Tropical Haze 》（1954年）展现了穿梭于绿色背景中的藤蔓状线条，人们不难想象这些线条取材于泽诺亲眼见过的绿植。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CZE059.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一幅描绘了一艘船从钻石拱门下方穿过的画作。", "caption": "科塞特·泽诺，《Safe Journey 》，1951年。摄影：查尔斯·鲁塞尔（Charles Roussel）", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她进入波多黎各大学时，正值该岛经历深刻变革的时期。1950年爆发的一系列反对美军的起义激发了波多黎各的民族主义精神，艺术家们也被动员起来推动自决精神。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在西班牙超现实主义者欧赫尼奥·格拉内尔（Eugenio Granell）的指导下——他的左翼政治立场曾迫使他在第二次世界大战期间从欧洲逃往加勒比地区——泽诺走上了一条与其他波多黎各艺术家不同的道路，将她关于争取独立的讯息编码进超现实主义的视觉语言中。她指向了《Safe article_text:
“This one over here is a weird one,” said Cossette Zeno , pointing to her 1952 painting Let’s Go Higher . Produced while she was still a student at the University of Puerto Rico in San Juan, the painting is a true oddity. It features an array of cubes in a largely vacant landscape set beneath a haze. A set of tiny people climb these angular modules, most of which have no windows or obvious function.

We met at Richard Saltoun’s New York gallery, where she is currently the subject of a small survey of her work from the 1950s. There, she drew my attention to the only cube depicted with a doorway in Let’s Go Higher . The green structure resembles a storage container emanating light. A single figure stands atop the cube proudly gesturing toward everything else around him. “He’s saying, ‘Always up, never down,’” Zeno said with a smile.

It’s an apt description of Zeno’s career, which spans nearly a century yet evaded global recognition until the past few years.

Zeno, 96, figured memorably in two major Surrealism surveys—one presenting a globalized version of the movement , which appeared at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Tate Modern between 2021 and 2022, and another exploring its Caribbean strain , which showed at the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth in Texas in 2024. Her latest showing, the Richard Saltoun show, is on view through Friday.

During the ’50s, Zeno forged a connection with André Breton, a cofounder of Surrealism, and exhibited alongside the movement’s adherents in Europe. Yet she never received canonization, perhaps because of her gender or because of the limited geographic focus of many Western art historians. Plus, as the scholar Whitney Chadwick has pointed out, many female Surrealists did not identify as members of the movement, in part because they felt alienated by their male counterparts. This sense of marginalization sidelined painters such as Meret Oppenheim, Leonora Carrington, and Remedios Varo, all of whom are now considered essential to Surrealist art history .

When I asked how she identified, however, she told me, “I call myself a Surrealist because I have their spirit of freedom. I have no fences. I am always evolving, baby!”

Her Surrealist spirit is abundantly evident in Ni hablar del peluquín (No Use to Talk about the Little Wig), the 1952 painting that featured in both institutional surveys. The painting features a monstrous tangle of flesh, with snatches of hair that might belong either to the titular toupee or to a more risqué part of the body.

“That represents a guy,” Zeno said. Nodding to the painting’s overt eroticism, she continued, “He’s thinking many things—you can decide what he’s thinking. He has a toupee, so he’s not a young guy.”

Male Surrealists like Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, and René Magritte were known for depicting the nude female body as a locus of desire and intrigue. Zeno, by contrast, estimated that she had only ever painted one naked woman. Why? “I like men,” she quipped.

Taking sips of beer, Zeno told me that works like this one were produced late at night. Still today, she’ll begin work at 11 p.m. and go to bed at 7 a.m. “Everybody who could bother me would be sleeping,” she said. “I’m free from cooking. I don’t have to clean the house.”

Many Surrealists likened their work to dreams, and that makes it notable that Zeno creates her work when others are in the REM stage of sleep. (This recalls a phrase once used by the Cuban Surrealist painter Wifredo Lam: “When I don’t sleep, I dream.”) Of her late-night art-making, Zeno told me, “I’m fully aware of what I’m doing.”

Zeno was born in the Dominican Republic in 1930, not long after the dictator Rafael Leónidas Trujillo seized power following a period of upheaval. When she was a toddler, Zeno and her family went into exile and left for Puerto Rico. “I don’t know Santo Domingo at all,” Zeno said. “That’s why I call myself Puerto Rican.”

In Old San Juan, Zeno took a liking to the mountains and sea all around her. “No matter where you stand in Puerto Rico, you see the ocean,” she said. “My grandmother used to take me to the ocean at 6 o’clock in the morning, so that I could see the little fish caught in the bubbles. I used to snorkel all the time.” Later, she added, “I’m very close to nature.”

Some of her earliest works reflect that. Two oil crayon drawings feature a mix of swirling white forms; they could represent shells tumbling through a current. (Zeno made them on paper she procured from her father’s business.) Tropical Haze (1954) features vine-like lines running through a greenish background, and it’s not hard to imagine they’re based on greenery Zeno encountered firsthand.

She entered the University of Puerto Rico at a time of profound change for the island. A series of revolts against the US military in 1950 helped galvanize the Puerto Rican nationalist spirit, and artists were enlisted to advance the spirit of self-determination.

Under the tutelage of Eugenio Granell, a Spanish Surrealist whose leftist politics had driven him to from Europe to the Caribbean during World War II, Zeno struck out in a different direction from other Puerto Rican artists, encoding her messages about the fight for independence in the visual language of Surrealism. She pointed to Safe Journey (1951), a painting in which a boat sails beneath a diamond arch. That arch, she said, signifies that “Puerto Rico is a poor country, but it’s not poor.” A fearsome beast reaches out to strike the boat, but it is blind, and so, she said, “there’s no threat. It has no power.”

After graduating from the University of Puerto Rico in 1953, Zeno received a postgraduate scholarship to study at the École du Louvre in Paris. There, she met Breton, whose influentialwas so great that she named one of her daughters after his 1928 book Nadja .

Her parents were living in Cuba at the time, and her father’s illness called her back to the Caribbean in 1954. More upheaval followed. She recalled being forced to leave Cuba twice. Once, while working for a textile company, she encountered a man bleeding out in the street and ran back to her job, where she warned a coworker of the reach of Fulgencio Batista’s regime; the employee ended up being a secret agent who urged her to leave Cuba expediently. Later, after marrying in the United States, she returned to visit her parents during the Castro era, only to find herself uprooted once more when he changed Cuba’s currency in 1961, rendering her money worthless.

Zeno has moved frequently over the years and is now based in Jackson, Missouri, where her granddaughter lives. She has never maintained a studio, she said, and there have been periods when she stopped painting altogether, including the year that her husband, Robert Bates, died.

But she is still working, and she excitedly told me about a new project: a painting spread across four full-size doors. Her grandson had initially asked her to paint a mural for the Atlanta hotel he’s opening, but she took the idea in a different direction. Working on the floor, Zeno is painting the doors with what she described as “sea elements.” This December, the doors will travel to Richard Saltoun’s booth at the Untitled Art, Miami Beach fair.

Her use of the doors recalls the portal in Let’s Go Higher , the painting with the unusually colored cubes. At one point in our interview, she reiterated her interpretation of the work: “You never go down, always up.”

article_text:
C hristoph Schlingensief certainly knew how to provoke. “Fury at German play that shows Queen as a Nazi,” read the Sunday Express’s headline after Kaprow City first premiered at Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre in 2006. Drawing on the happenings of US performance artist Allan Kaprow, the play turned its attention to Diana, Princess of Wales’s death. In one scene, the then queen performs a Hitler salute. Another re-enacts the paparazzi chase that led to Diana’s fatal crash. Diana appears in bed beside two men with Down’s syndrome; and Camilla is pelted with animal blood. Schlingensief insisted the work was not meant as provocation but as an investigation into how Diana turned into a modern icon. But his art thrived on outrage, exposing the absurdity of societies that glorify their idols while consuming their lives as entertainment.

Kaprow City is at the heart of a new Berlin show – It’s Not My Problem Anymore, Deal With Your Own Shit – that revisits the artist’s legacy. In the Gropius Bau’s grand neo-Renaissance atrium, visitors encounter remnants of the carousel-like rotating stage he called the “animatograph”. Looking at this installation today feels like a glimpse into Schlingensief’s mind: a messy collage of childhood memories, violent fantasies and royal glamour.

The Gropius Bau installed roughly half of Schlingensief’s original set on the very same spot where Joseph Beuys, a major influence, once exhibited his Stag Monuments. In Kaprow City, flickering black-and-white footage of a crucifixion plays beneath a slate board listing the stage’s contents, from “Diana Girl Ballet” to “exorcism”. In the original production, audiences were distributed across 18 tiny, wedge-shaped rooms, echoing Allan Kaprow’s 18 Happenings in 6 Parts. Spectators witnessed only fragments of the action. Now, most of the stage’s interior is draped in plastic. Excerpts of videos from the play loop throughout the installation on old-fashioned TV screens.

Enlarged tabloid headlines and articles are plastered across the walls behind it. Beside the Sunday Express headline, a German newspaper asks: “Will Diana’s sons stop Schlingensief?” After rumours that the royals might pursue legal action, Schlingensief had invited William and Harry to Frieze, where he planned to present an iteration of the project.

“The combination of Lady Di, the speculation surrounding the circumstances of her death, and the general myth that grew around her fascinated Christoph,” says stage designer Aino Laberenz, Schlingensief’s widow who now manages his estate. For the Volksbühne production, Schlingensief cast Jenny Elvers, a German TV personality whose private life, like Diana’s, was a fixture of tabloids, between fascination and intense scrutiny. Laberenz cautions against viewing Kaprow City only through the lens of Diana. It belonged to a wider artistic universe in which theatre, film and art collided and overlapped with questions of media power and spectacle, she says.

Schlingensief, who died of lung cancer just shy of his 50th birthday in 2010, grew up in the shadow of New German Cinema and was deeply influenced by film-makers such as Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Like Fassbinder, he blurred the lines between art and politics. In The African Twin Towers, he took actors including Patti Smith, Irm Hermann and Robert Stadlober to Namibia to re-enact Wagnerian myths, confronting the legacy of Germany’s colonial genocide. Namibian actors also took part.

Seen today, Schlingensief’s artistic vocabulary – messy B-movie horror, drag, disabled performers, a taste for the extreme – sits awkwardly with Namibia as a stage. Watching his actors improvise on Shark Island, the site of a former German concentration camp where Herero and Nama prisoners endured forced labour and starvation, feels uncomfortable. Not because the provocation is empty (it isn’t), but because one wonders whether the team fully grasped what they were doing. Namibia feels less like the subject of a reckoning with Germany’s colonial past than a backdrop for a German artist’s grand vision. At Gropius Bau, The African Twin Towers appears as a patchwork of sequences across 18 screens.

Schlingensief’s work on the far right, however, remains strikingly relevant – not only because of the AfD’s rise in Germany, but also because of his hands-on confrontational approach to anti-immigrant politics. In his version of Hamlet, he brought former far-right extremists on to the stage at Schauspielhaus Zürich and later Berlin’s Volksbühne, where they re-enacted Shakespeare’s central murder scene amid far-right rock music and Nazi aesthetics. “We’re not playing Hamlet, we’re playing Germany,” reads a Schlingensief quote taped to the exhibition wall. It captures the artist’s insistence that art must confront society, rather than offer an escape.

The same attitude runs through Ausländer Raus! Schlingensiefs Container, his 2000 project in which asylum seekers lived under surveillance in a Big Brother-style container beside Vienna’s State Opera, while audiences voted on who should be deported first, two people a day. Conceived in response to the far-right FPÖ’s entry into Austria’s government, the project turned deportation – or, in the AfD’s words, “remigration” – into an eerie spectacle. It exposed European racism while implicating viewers in its public reproduction.

Looking at these works today, one cannot help thinking of how far-right actors have learned to adopt such aesthetic spectacle as a political tool. The AfD’s AI video Remigration Hit from 2024, for instance, revels in humiliating migrant men herded on to planes by Aryan-looking pilots. Schlingensief’s work reads as a warning of how easily such cruelty becomes entertainment. And how readily the media help normalise it, from the tabloid frenzy surrounding Diana to the far right’s supremacist language of “remigration”.

“I keep noticing in the commentary how much he is missed,” says Laberenz toward the end of our interview. “But I also like to say that it’s up to us, whether we work in the arts or not, not to hand responsibility over to someone else so that we no longer have to act.”

可怕的B电影恐怖,拖动,残疾演员,极端的味道 - 与纳米比亚作为一个场景坐得很可怕。 观看他的演员在沙尔克岛上 improvises,前德国集中营的场所,在那里赫雷罗和纳马囚犯坚持强迫劳动和饥饿,感觉不舒服。纳米比亚感觉不到德国殖民过去的计算,而不是德国艺术家的伟大愿景的背景。在Gropius Bau,非洲双胞胎塔出现在18个屏幕上的序列的模具。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而,施林内西夫对远右的作品仍然非常有意义,不仅是因为德国的阿富汗反对派的崛起,而且是因为他对反移民政治的对抗态度。在哈姆雷特的版本中,他引进了前远右派极端分子在苏黎世 Schauspielhaus和后来柏林的Volksbühne,在那里他们在远右摇滚音乐和纳粹美学中重新启动了莎士比亚的中央谋杀场景。哈姆雷特,我们正在玩德国,“在展览墙上写着施林内西夫的引用,这引用了艺术家坚持艺术必须面对社会,而不是提供逃避。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/14fb5976f24e6028b20a13b661c418e5e172437c/0_0_2500_1667/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "一个小教堂建在一个大画廊空间内", "caption": "《他有多想念》......克里斯托夫·施林森西夫,恐惧教会,2003年,《不再是我的问题》的一部分,处理你的自己的阴影。", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "同样的态度是通过 Ausländer Raus! article_text:
Può succedere sfogliando una serie di vecchie cartoline che conservano frammenti di vita – scritti in quella tipica calligrafia di un tempo – dietro un’immagine in bianco e nero; può accadere provando una giacca sartoriale; tra stoviglie e complementi d’arredo, riconoscendo un oggetto simile a quello che veniva usato la domenica nella casa dei propri nonni; o ancora quando si trova proprio quella lampada di design che si cercava da mesi, da mettere accanto a una pila di libri nel salone: i mercatini vintage, di antiquariato e modernariato fungono a volte da portali per scoprire, per cercare qualcosa che spesso non si sa bene cos’è; e poi – magari – si capisce che si cercava tutt’altro. I mercatini vintage funzionano anche così: mettono in circolazione frammenti di vite precedenti e li affidano a chi saprà riconoscerne il valore.

In un mercato dominato dalla disponibilità immediata delle merci e dalla continua uscita di nuovi prodotti, il vintage introduce una temporalità differente. Bisogna guardare, confrontare, rovistare e, talvolta, tornare a casa a mani vuote.

Il prossimo fine settimana offre diverse occasioni per esplorare questo universo, da Nord a Sud. Dall’antiquariato di qualità nel cuore di Venezia ai capi vintage di Milano e Parma, passando per il collezionismo di Modena e la creatività indipendente di Roma, gli appuntamenti in calendario restituiscono un panorama variegato, nel quale convivono ricerca estetica e passione per il second hand.

Venezia: il Mercatino dell’antiquariato di Campo San Maurizio

Dal 16 al 18 ottobre, Campo San Maurizio torna a ospitare il Mercatino dell’antiquariato , appuntamento che da più di cinquant’anni e con oltre sessanta espositori antiquari da tutta Italia porta nel centro storico veneziano una selezione di oggetti d’epoca, modernariato e curiosità da collezione. Per tre giorni, dalle 9 alle 19, il campo si trasforma in un percorso tra materiali e storie che attraversano epoche differenti. L’offerta comprende antiquariato, libri antichi, stampe, vetri, ceramiche, gioielli vintage e oggettistica d’epoca. Accanto agli espositori italiani sono annunciati operatori provenienti da Croazia e Slovenia, con proposte che ampliano la dimensione internazionale del mercato e offrono ulteriori occasioni di ricerca a collezionisti e appassionati.

A Venezia , dove il rapporto tra oggetti, artigianato e tradizione materiale è parte integrante della storia cittadina, il mercatino si inserisce in uno spazio urbano che invita a rallentare e a osservare: il modernariato e il vintage dialogano qui con una cultura del fare e del conservare che comprende il vetro, la ceramica, la stampa e le arti decorative.

Modena: COLLEZIONANDO e il vintage

Il 17 e 18 ottobre il quartiere fieristico di Modena ospita COLLEZIONANDO , manifestazione dedicata al collezionismo che riunisce ambiti diversi, dalla musica al fumetto, fino al vintage e alle figurine. Aperta dalle 9 alle 19, la fiera si rivolge tanto ai collezionisti esperti quanto a chi si avvicina per la prima volta alla ricerca di oggetti da conservare o rimettere in circolazione. Per chi è interessato alla moda e al design, l’area vintage propone abbigliamento d’epoca, accessori, occhiali, borse, bijoux e oggetti di modernariato, permettendo di osservare come forme e dettagli tornino periodicamente a essere riletti dalle tendenze contemporanee. La particolarità di COLLEZIONANDO consiste, però, proprio nella convivenza tra differenti forme di collezionismo: accanto a capi e complementi d’arredo trovano spazio vinili, prime stampe, edizioni limitate, fumetti, tavole originali e raccolte di figurine.

Milano: East Market, tra second hand e modernariato

Domenica 18 ottobre torna anche East Market , in un’ex fabbrica aeronautica in via Mecenate a Milano, con una giornata dedicata al vintage, al second hand e al modernariato. Ogni edizione coinvolge circa 300 espositori provenienti da tutta Italia, con un’offerta che attraversa abbigliamento e accessori d’epoca, antiquariato, sneakers, vinili, oggetti curiosi e vecchie collezioni. L’appuntamento si tiene in uno spazio coperto di circa 3.000 metri quadrati, attrezzato per accogliere il pubblico in ogni stagione. Accanto alle bancarelle, il Food Market propone specialità gastronomiche internazionali, mentre dal pomeriggio i dj set accompagnano la visita, trasformando la ricerca tra gli espositori in un’esperienza che si prolunga oltre lo shopping.

Visualizza questo post su Instagram Un post condiviso da East Market {Milano} (@eastmarketmilano)

Parma e Milano con Remira Market: la cultura del riuso incontra la creatività indipendente

Il fine settimana di Remira Market si articola in due appuntamenti distinti: sabato 17 ottobre il mercato arriva a La Galleria, in via Emilia Est 7B a Parma , mentre domenica 18 si sposta a Milano, nel cortile del Teatro Cinema Martinitt, in via Pitteri 58.

In entrambi gli appuntamenti, il vintage viene presentato come una possibilità concreta di ripensare il rapporto con ciò che si acquista. La selezione degli espositori, la presenza di produzioni indipendenti, e l’attenzione all’ upcycling e alla sostenibilità raccontano un interesse per modalità di consumo nelle quali originalità e riuso possono procedere insieme, diventando parte di uno stile di vita più consapevole. Il risultato è un mercato che si rivolge sia a chi cerca un capo particolare sia a chi vuole scoprire realtà creative al di fuori dei circuiti commerciali più convenzionali.

Roma: La Domenica Vintage al Monk

Domenica 18 ottobre, il Monk Roma , in via Giuseppe Mirri 35, ospita La Domenica Vintage , appuntamento a ingresso gratuito dedicato al vintage, al riuso, all’handmade e alla creatività indipendente. La proposta comprende abbigliamento e accessori vintage, vinili, illustrazioni, produzioni artigianali, brand indipendenti e oggetti unici, costruendo un percorso tra linguaggi creativi differenti. Accanto alla ricerca di capi e accessori d’epoca, il pubblico può incontrare illustratori, artigiani e confrontarsi con piccoli progetti indipendenti, in una dimensione che avvicina il commercio alla scoperta e alla relazione diretta con chi produce o seleziona gli oggetti.

La scelta del Monk, spazio culturale aperto a progetti indipendenti e sperimentazioni artistiche, contribuisce a definire il carattere dell’appuntamento: il market si inserisce in un luogo che fa della musica e della condivisione una parte importante della propria identità, e che per l’occasione affianca alla ricerca tra gli espositori la possibilità di trascorrere l’intera giornata tra gli spazi espositivi, con food e drink disponibili sul luogo. La Domenica Vintage va quindi a intercettare una dimensione del riuso che non riguarda soltanto la circolazione di merci già esistenti, ma anche la costruzione di comunità temporanee intorno a interessi condivisi.

Il valore di ciò che continua a circolare

I mercatini del vintage mettono in discussione, anche senza proclami, una delle convinzioni più radicate nella società dei consumi: ciò che è nuovo è migliore, e il valore di un oggetto d’uso diminuisce con il passare del tempo. Non tutto ciò che è vecchio merita di essere conservato, naturalmente, e non ogni compera second hand è automaticamente sostenibile. Ogni acquisto sottrae qualcosa all’oblio, ma apre anche una possibilità diversa, quella di inserire un frammento del passato in un contesto nuovo, lontano da quello per cui era stato pensato. E in questo passaggio – ancor più che nella nostalgia per ciò che è stato – il vintage trova una parte della sua fortuna e del suo significato contemporaneo.

article_text:
金沢21世紀美術館、長期休館を前にエルメスと特別プログラムを開催。「作品の継承」を問い直す

2027年5月から長期休館に入る 金沢21世紀美術館 が、 エルメス ジャポンと共同でワークショップとシンポジウムを開催する。現代美術作品を未来へどう受け継ぐのか、保存修復やものづくりの視点から考える。

金沢21世紀美術館 では、長期休館前の最後の展覧会「 今日から明日へ 作品を継承すること 」が10月31日から開幕する（2027年4月18日まで）。その関連プログラムとして、 エルメス ジャポンとともに、ワークショップとシンポジウム「壊れていくもの、継承していくもの」を11月に開催する予定だ。

展覧会「今日から明日へ 作品を継承すること」は、2004年の開館以来の歩みを振り返り、作品を未来へどう残していくのかという問いに向き合う。同館が収集してきた4000点超のコレクションのうち、保存・修復や展示方法の検討を要する作品を中心に取り上げる。コレクションには絵画や彫刻に加え、メディアアート、観客の参加や上演によって成立する作品なども含まれ、素材の経年変化や機材の旧式化、展示環境の変化など、その継承には多くの不確実性が伴う。こうした継承のあり方を考える上で一例となるのが、 宮永愛子 の《waiting for awakening -chair-》（2012）だ。素材のナフタリンが昇華し、次第に形を失っていくこの作品は、元の状態を保つことだけではないという作品の継承のあり方を考える。

本企画は、エルメスジャポンと金沢21世紀美術館が2024年から続けてきた協働を発展させたものだ。両者はこれまで、能登への支援や、アートを介した職人の技術と手仕事の継承に取り組んできた。こうした活動を踏まえ、今回は展覧会で掲げられた作品の修復と継承という問いを、アート、保存修復、ものづくりの視点から掘り下げる。

第1部のワークショップは、保存修復を手がかりに「作品を未来へ継承するために、何を残し、どのような変化を受け入れるのか」を考える内容だ。キュレーターズツアーとグループワークの2部構成で、専門知識の有無を問わず18歳以上であれば参加できる。11月1日または8日に同館で行われるキュレーターズツアーでは、保存修復の観点から展示作品を鑑賞し、継承について考えたい作品を参加者がそれぞれ選ぶ。続く11月13日には金沢美術工芸大学でグループワークを実施。参加者が持ち寄った考えをもとに、保存に困難が伴う作品や、現状を維持することを目的としていない作品が抱える課題について議論する。その後、各グループが1作品を選んで議論の内容を発表し、修復家で京都大学准教授の田口かおりがコメントを寄せる。

11月14日には、第2部のシンポジウムが金沢21世紀美術館で開催される。登壇するのは、修復家の田口かおり、彫刻の保存修復に携わりながら制作も行うアーティストの髙橋銑、インストーラーの有元利彦、アーティストの野村大輔、エルメスジャポン取締役会長の有賀昌男、金沢21世紀美術館館長の鷲田めるろの6人。ミクスト・メディアやメディアアート、インスタレーションなど、従来の保存修復の枠組みでは捉えきれない現代美術作品をどのように未来へ継承するのかについて議論する。モデレーターは同館学芸課長の角奈緒子が務める。なお、髙橋は本展のゲストアーティストとしても新作を発表する。さらにシンポジウムでは、エミール・エルメス・コレクションとスカーフのものづくりを通して、エルメスが受け継いできた修復と継承の思想が紹介される。

「壊れていくもの、継承していくもの」

title_original: Wildwood Review: Magic and Terror on a Breathtaking Scale
editorial_title_zh: 《Wildwood》评论：魔法与恐怖的壮丽呈现
editorial_excerpt_zh: 注：本文最初是作为我们2026年伦敦电影节报道的一部分发表的。这部电影将于10月23日上映。由于《鬼妈妈》（Coraline），这是LAIKA作为工作室的首次尝试，至今仍是其最著名的作品，因此人们期望每一部后续作品都能舒适地融入恐怖领域，每一部新作品都成为数千名此前不知电影能让他们做噩梦的孩子们的必经之路。《Wildwood》也将不可避免地如此，这是导演特拉维斯·奈特（Travis Knight）对2011年《Decemberists》主唱科林·梅洛（Colin Meloy）的青少年小说的奢华而雄心勃勃的改编，尤其是因为它以一个年轻男孩自杀开场，扯出自己的内脏，揭示他其实是一个由齿轮驱动的机械人。哥特式意象从那以后几乎没有减退，奈特很快重现了希区柯克电影《鸟》（The Birds）中的令人难忘的画面，一群乌鸦蜂拥而至，准备袭击毫无防备的孩子们。

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 BFI London coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 23.

Because of Coraline , LAIKA’s first effort as a studio and still its best-known, there’s an expectation that each subsequent project will fit comfortably within the horror realm, each new release a rite of passage for thousands of kids previously unaware that movies could give them nightmares. This will inevitably be the same case with Wildwood , director Travis Knight’s lavish and ambitious adaptation of the 2011 YA novel by Decemberists lead singer Colin Meloy, not least because it cold-opens with a young boy committing suicide, ripping out his insides to reveal he was an automaton operated by cogs. The gothic imagery hardly subsides from there, with Knight soon recreating the haunting image from Hitchcock’s The Birds , a murder of crows swarming over a playground ready to feast on unsuspecting children.

Labelling a LAIKA production a straightforward riff on horror hasn’t been accurate since 2012’s Paranorman ––their weakest, most surface-level referential effort––with the studio’s work since then better appreciated as part of an ongoing attempt to revive other genres unfashionable with today’s kids. It’s won them as much acclaim as it has come at a cost; Missing Link , their 2019 globe-trotting adventure that’s partway between Jules Verne and The Lost City of Z , holds the title for most expensive stop-motion film of all-time, and made the smallest fraction of that cost back.

Wildwood might be an easier sell as a modern-day fairytale, but it doesn’t make any concessions to what children might want or expect from such a proposition—more Brothers Grimm by way of Tolkien than Disney. If it does have a contemporary parallel, it’s with the equally dark, unsanitized female empowerment tales of Hayao Miyazaki, where wonder and grimness co-exist as they did in the oldest bedtime stories. Characters are shaped forever by the darkness they encounter as much as they are thrilled by any fantastical, otherworldly creatures who cross their path, all of whom are crafted with an attention to detail unrivaled within their respective forms of animation.

After the prologue, we head to modern-day Portland, where Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) has been tasked with babysitting her baby brother Mac, advised by her hippie parents (Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine) not to take him outside. It’s a rule she breaks often, but their carefree trip into the city that morning ends in disaster when crows swarm over her brother in the playground and whisk him off to the vast woods surrounding the city. Along with nerdy classmate Curtis (Jacob Tremblay), they venture into the unknown, even though they’ve long been warned that the overgrown forests are impossible to enter.

Mysteriously, a path opens for the pair, who are soon separated after encountering an anthropomorphic coyote army; Prue makes it to a nearby town, where she’s held captive as an outsider. Jacob is taken to meet the former governess Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) who, instead of treating him as a captive, sees him as a replacement for the long-dead son of whom she’s repeatedly tried to build a replica. Alexandra is holding baby Mac for sinister reasons just as tensions among the different clans in the woods have grown worse due to the actions of her army; saving her brother means having to save the realm from her.

There’s an eeriness to Wildwood that never becomes fully fleshed horror, toeing the line when it comes to the limits of darkness in a fairytale; it earns its PG-13 rating before we’re even a minute into the runtime, and that’s just Knight testing the waters of acceptability. It’s easy to write this off as the director and his screenwriter Chris Butler targeting a slightly older audience who are weaned on campfire ghost stories and on the cusp of seeing their first scary movie at a sleepover, but as with Miyazaki’s coming-of-age tales, I see this as the distinct work of creatives who trust their young viewers’ intelligence, knowing that they can handle something darker than what’s offered by rival animation studios. It’s only because it’s in stop-motion that this darkness is presented as novel.

Adaptations of Tolkien, C.S. Lewis, and other widely read fantasy authors from most people’s childhoods have been embraced by young viewers, after all, and in its character designs and staging of sweeping action sequences, Wildwood frequently invites the lofty comparisons to Peter Jackson’s original Lord of the Rings trilogy that it manages to live up to. Yes, it’s on a smaller scale because of the limits of a team of stop-motion animators, but that a battle scene can feel positively reminiscent of Jackson’s Helm’s Deep––even when it pauses to breathe amidst the chaos to show how the violence may scar its characters forever––is one of several technical achievements that don’t call themselves out as such. The soaring aerial sequences, gag-a-minute slapstick chase scenes, and transformation of the sets as reeds quickly grow on every surface represent some of the most ambitious moments the studio has ever put to life. In the moment, it’s easy to look past how the enormous scale of this ambition is paying off; the movie satisfies the heart so much that the head stops seeking to work out how they did it.

The majority of LAIKA efforts close with a mid-credits, behind-the-scenes look at the painstaking work that went into creating their character models and expansive sets. As much as they want you to be transported into their lovingly crafted worlds, they’re magicians who have no issues revealing their secrets, and part of the charm of Wildwood is seeing just how the sausage gets made before heading to the exit. We’re in a period where studio animation is becoming increasingly risk-averse, and there’s something oddly moving about seeing a member of Knight’s team walk us through the process of designing characters.

The movie may not resonate with younger audiences or even attract many of them into the theater to begin with, but just like the famous line about how the few who first heard The Velvet Underground & Nico formed their own bands, it offers the hope that the kids who do see it will be inspired to make art of their own. For anybody older, it’s a reminder of the magic and terror of the classic fantasy stories we grew up with recaptured on a breathtaking scale. It’s among the best animated films in recent memory.

Wildwood premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival and opens on October 23.

article_text:
Patrick Stewart ‘s final movie role will be in the upcoming “ Avengers: Doomsday ,” which marks his ninth time playing the “X-Men” character Charles Xavier on the big screen. Marvel Studios confirmed the news in their tribute to the late actor, who died at 86 years old after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia.

“Stewart made his debut as Professor X in 2000’s ‘X-Men,’ where he embodied the composure, class, and wisdom of the beloved telepathic mutant and mentor of the X-Men,” Marvel Studios wrote in a tribute. “For more than 25 years, he brought a gravitas and profundity to the [character]… He returned to the role once more with 2026’s ‘Avengers: Doomsday,’ his final on-screen appearance.”

Related Stories

Dawn Porter to Direct Documentary on Pioneering TV News Anchor Max Robinson

In between “X-Men” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” Stewart popped up as Charles Xavier in various Marvel sequels, prequels and reboots such as 2003’s “X2: X-Men United,” 2006’s “X-Men: The Last Stand,” 2009’s “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” 2013’s “The Wolverine,” 2014’s “X-Men: Days of Future Past,” and 2017’s acclaimed “Logan.” The role, along with Captain Picard in the “Star Trek” franchise, will go down as Stewart’s most iconic screen character.

“We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today,” Stewart’s longtime “X-Men” co-star Hugh Jackman wrote on Instagram in a tribute. “And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

In one of Stewart’s now-final interviews published by TV Insider in July, the actor spoke about his decision to return as Charles Xavier in “Avengers: Doomsday” and told fans that he would never “retire” from acting.

“As any actor my age will tell you, there are fewer and fewer available roles as we get older. That being said, I still continue to receive interesting offers and I love being challenged by new work,” Stewart said at the time. “I can’t imagine ever officially retiring. I’ll always and forever be an actor.”

Marvel Studios put out its own statement mourning the loss of Stewart by saying the company is “deeply saddened” by his passing, adding: “Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from ‘X- Men’ to ‘Logan’ to ‘Avengers: Doomsday.’ He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman.”

“We’ve been lucky enough to work with some of our childhood heroes. And Sir Patrick Stewart will always be one of them,” added “Avengers: Doomsday” directors Joe and Anthony Russo in their own statement. “A legendary actor with an unmistakeable presence, and an unmatched integrity. Thank you for entertaining all of us, sir. And for teaching us humanity, both on and off the screen.”

“Avengers: Doomsday” opens in theaters Dec. 18 from Disney and Marvel Studios.

article_text:
カリフォルニア ・モダニズムの先駆者、 建築 家ルドルフ・シンドラー（Rudolph Schindler、1887–1953）の代表作、ロヴェル・ビーチ・ハウス（Lovell Beach House）が1880万ドル（約29億7000万円）で 売りに出されている 。1926年の竣工以来、100年にわたって同じ一族に受け継がれてきた海辺の名住宅だ。

オーストリアで建築を学んだシンドラーは渡米後、 フランク・ロイド・ライト の設計事務所で経験を積んだ。1920年から1953年まで南カリフォルニアで活動し、 ロサンゼルス 各地で住宅や集合住宅など100件以上を設計。この地の近代建築の発展に大きく貢献した。

「住む人をより健康にする住宅を」

ニューポートビーチのバルボア半島に位置するロヴェル・ビーチ・ハウスは、自然療法家フィリップ・ロヴェル（Philip Lovell）の依頼で建てられた。ロサンゼルス・タイムズ紙に健康コラム「Care of the Body」を執筆していたロヴェルは、菜食や運動、新鮮な空気、裸での日光浴を重視し、屋外で眠ることも健康によいと信じていた。彼にとって住宅は、単に風雨をしのぐ場所ではなく、住む人をより健康にするためのものだった。

その信念から、ロヴェルは寝室の代わりに外気に開かれた就寝用ポーチを設けるよう求めた。シンドラーは屋上に日光浴用のテラスを設計し、浴室には約5個のシャワーヘッドからの流水を、横になったまま浴びられる独特な設備も取り入れた。だが、屋外で眠る試みが続いたのは、わずか2年ほど。ニューポートビーチの夜の冷え込みと霧にはかなわず、1928年にはシンドラーがポーチを囲い、通常の寝室へと改修した。

リビングの様子。ビーチに面した大きな窓が特徴的だ。Photo: Sterling Reed

ロヴェル・ビーチ・ハウスからの眺め。Photo: Sterling Reed

建築当時からの造り付けの棚や家具は、そのまま残されている。Photo: Sterling Reed

ロヴェル・ビーチ・ハウス外観。Photo: Sterling Reed

この住宅の外観を特徴づけるのは、角張った「8」の字に似た巨大なコンクリート製フレーム5基だ。居住空間を地上から持ち上げることで、浜辺を行き交う人々の視線から家族のプライバシーを守りつつ、太平洋を一望できるようにしている。

現在は寝室とバスルームがそれぞれ4室あり、2層吹き抜けのリビングルームには、その空間を見下ろすバルコニーが張り出す。床面積は約255平方メートルで、今日の同価格帯の海辺の住宅としては、それほど広くはない。もっとも、買い手が対価を払うのは、単なる広さではないだろう。

秘められた2人の建築家の確執

この住宅には、近代建築のもう1人の巨匠も関わっている。後にシンドラーのライバルとなるリチャード・ノイトラ（Richard Neutra、1892-1970）が、造園を手がけたのだ。2人はかつて友人であり、協働する仲でもあったが、やがて関係は悪化した。

ロヴェル夫妻の選択も、その一因となった。夫妻は海辺の住宅をシンドラーに依頼した後、ロサンゼルスの自邸、ロヴェル・ヘルス・ハウス（Lovell Health House）の設計をノイトラに任せた。1929年に完成したこの住宅は、ノイトラの名声を確立する一助となる一方、2人の建築家の間に亀裂を生むことにもなった。

一族が100年守り続けた名建築

建築史に名を刻むビーチ・ハウスは、一家の暮らしの場でもあった。フィリップと妻のリアは、やがてここを生活の拠点とし、さまざまなアーティストや知識人を招いた。写真家のエドワード・ウェストン（Edward Weston）も訪れており、一族によれば、歌手で俳優のポール・ロブスン（Paul Robeson）がリビングルームで歌声を披露したこともあったという。

住宅はその後、ロヴェル家の数世代にわたって受け継がれた。1970年代初頭には、夫妻の末息子ゲイリーが父と兄から約5万ドル（現在の為替で約790万円）で取得。妻のバーバラとともに、キッチンを開放的な間取りに変え、もともとあった大きな浴室を2つに分けるなど、いくつかの変更を加えた。バーバラは2025年に亡くなるまで、ここで暮らし続けた。

こうした改修を経ても、一族は造り付け家具を含め、シンドラーの当初の設計を多くの部分で守ってきた。住宅は1974年にアメリカの国家歴史登録財（National Register of Historic Places）に登録され、建築愛好家が訪れる名所となっている。ロヴェル夫妻の孫たちによれば、写真撮影やスケッチのため、大勢の見学者がバスで訪れることも珍しくないという。

だが、一家がこの家を愛した理由は、もっとシンプルなものだった。1958年、建築史家エスター・マッコイの取材に応じたリアは、ノイトラが手がけた、より有名なロサンゼルスの自邸よりも、シンドラーの海辺の家を好む理由をこう語った。

「私たちに、ぴったりだったんです」

竣工から100年を迎えた今、この家は新たに「ぴったり」と感じてくれる誰かを探している。できれば1880万ドルを用意でき、建築の歴史、そして、ときに肌寒い海風を愛せる人を。（翻訳：編集部）

優れた美術館が備えるべき条件とは何だろう？ それは内部に展示されている作品だけではなく、美術品を収める建物も重要だ。多くの建築家が、美術館もアートとして鑑賞の対象になりうると認識しており、所蔵されている傑作と同じくらい建築そのものが広く知られている美術館も少なくない。ここでは、過去100年間に建てられた 美術館 のうち、それ自体が最も重要な芸術作品といえる25の建築を紹介する。
